title: Impact budgétaire pour la France de l'accord « side-by-side » sur l'impôt minimum mondial (Pilier 2) et exonération des multinationales américaines
date_evidence:
Question publiée le 23/04/2026

## Question de Mme BLATRIX CONTAT Florence (Ain - SER) publiée le 23/04/2026

Publiée dans le JO Sénat du 23/04/2026 - page 1918
key_claim: A French Senate written question records that the 5 January 2026 side-by-side accord effectively exempts US multinationals from the 15% global minimum tax, cites a TaxWatch UK estimate of roughly $40.5 billion in annual worldwide revenue loss, and reports first national estimates of a 30% reduction in expected Pillar Two receipts for the United Kingdom (about £700 million) and about 26% for the Netherlands, with no published French estimate.
frame_summary: This source argues that the side-by-side accord transfers a quantifiable fiscal cost onto non-US implementing states and that the French government has not yet disclosed the national revenue impact, making the asymmetry a question of budgetary accountability and of the integrity of the minimum-tax regime.
verbatim_quote: Une récente analyse de l'organisation TaxWatch UK estime à environ 40,5 milliards de dollars annuels la perte de recettes fiscales mondiale imputable à ce dispositif. Les premières évaluations nationales disponibles font état d'une réduction d'environ 30 % des recettes attendues au titre du Pilier 2 pour le Royaume-Uni, soit environ 700 millions de livres sterling, et d'environ 26 % pour les Pays-Bas.
verbatim_list: les prévisions de recettes françaises au titre du Pilier 2 avaient déjà été très sensiblement révisées à la baisse entre 2023 et 2025, passant de 1,5 milliard d'euros à environ 500 millions d'euros
notes: Structural anchor and the French-language primary source satisfying the multi-language sourcing rule for an EU-anchored topic. A parliamentary written question, so the figures are the questioner's citations of TaxWatch UK and of national estimates, not government-verified numbers; the body attributes them accordingly. title: Competitive Corporate Tax Policy Is Essential for European Economic Growth
date_evidence: Competitive Corporate Tax Policy Is Essential for European Economic Growth ... Europe May 21, 2026 May 20, 2026
key_claim: Tax Foundation Europe argues that a decade of European tax debate centred on fairness and anti-avoidance is being displaced by competitiveness and growth objectives under geoeconomic pressure.
frame_summary: This source argues that European corporate tax policy should now be judged by its effect on investment and growth rather than by anti-avoidance criteria, and that geoeconomic competition is what is forcing the reorientation.

title: EU taxes on digital services, gambling, crypto could yield up to 11 billion euro per year, Commission says
key_claim: A Commission document shared with member states estimates that new EU-level taxes on digital services, online gambling and crypto assets could raise almost 11 billion euro a year for the 2028-2034 budget, with the digital levy alone estimated at about 5 billion euro on a 3% rate.
frame_summary: This source argues that the EU is actively shopping for new own resources and that digital-services taxation is back on the table as budget financing rather than as a fairness measure, despite the unresolved international dispute over such levies.
verbatim_quote: The European Commission estimates the next EU budget could benefit from almost €11bn in additional yearly revenues from new taxes on digital services, gambling and crypto assets, according to a document shared with EU member states and seen by Euronews.
verbatim_list: For a digital tax, the Commission calculated the EU could receive approximately €5bn annually, based on 2024 revenues from Spain, France and Italy, all of which already levy a tax on digital services.
notes: Reporting on a leaked Commission working document; figures are Commission estimates, not adopted proposals. Provenance audit unverifiable in-sandbox; re-run host-side.

title: Testimony: Are Digital Services Taxes a Viable Solution for the EU Budget?
date_evidence:
# Testimony: Are Digital Services Taxes a Viable Solution for the EU Budget?

June 23, 2026June 22, 2026By: Cristina Enache
key_claim: Testimony to the European Parliament Committee on Budgets records that 10 European countries have implemented digital services taxes with rates from 1.5% to 7.5% and widely differing bases, and argues that this lack of harmonisation has created complexity and fragmentation across the Single Market.
frame_summary: This source argues that digital services taxes are an economically poor instrument that raises little revenue, falls on consumers and invites retaliation, and that the EU should strengthen VAT instead of adding a bloc-wide digital levy.
verbatim_quote: In fact, 10 countries—Austria, Denmark, France, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Turkey, and the UK—have implemented a DST.
verbatim_list: This lack of harmonization has created complexity and fragmentation across the Single Market.
Tax rates also vary quite a bit—ranging from 1.5 percent in Poland to 7.5 percent in Hungary and Turkey.
notes: Written testimony submitted to the European Parliament Committee on Budgets on 23 June 2026. Advocacy position is explicit and disclosed in the body framing. Provenance audit unverifiable in-sandbox; re-run host-side.

title: European Commission proposes landmark tax simplification package to streamline compliance and boost competitiveness
date_evidence:
- News article
- 24 June 2026
- Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union

On 24 June 2026, the European Commission adopted an ambitious tax simplification package
key_claim: The Commission's 24 June 2026 direct taxation Omnibus and DAC recast are estimated to cut business compliance costs by approximately EUR 7.9 billion, and remove DAC6 cross-border arrangement reporting for around 3,000 multinational groups already inside the 15% global minimum tax, saving 300 million euro a year.
frame_summary: This source argues that the EU's priority in direct taxation is now simplification and competitiveness, framing reduced compliance obligations, including for groups already inside Pillar Two, as the way to make Europe a more attractive place to invest.
verbatim_quote: The package is estimated to bring savings and reduce compliance costs for business by approximately EUR 7.9 billion.
verbatim_list: The recast removes reporting requirements on cross-border tax arrangements for approximately 3,000 multinational enterprise groups that are already subject to the 15% global minimum tax under Pillar Two rules, generating annual compliance cost savings of €300 million.
notes: Primary EU legislative-proposal record. Provenance audit unverifiable in-sandbox; re-run host-side.

date_evidence:

# European Union: European Commission Publishes EU Tax Simplification Package
key_claim: Baker McKenzie records that the Omnibus proposal offers targeted CFC exemptions for groups in scope of Pillar Two and a DAC6 reporting exemption for those groups, and that both instruments require unanimous approval by all EU member states, leaving adoption uncertain.
frame_summary: This source argues that the EU package is a taxpayer-friendly competitiveness measure whose practical effect is uncertain because unanimity is required, and advises multinationals to test whether the proposals would improve their tax and financing positions.
verbatim_quote: The Omnibus Proposal is intended to enhance competitiveness, reduce tax compliance burdens and simplify cross-border operations within the EU.
verbatim_list: The Omnibus Proposal and recast of the DAC will require unanimous approval from all EU Member States. Therefore, it is uncertain if, or to what extent, the proposed amendments will be implemented, also considering budgetary implications.
notes: Law-firm client alert used for the legal mechanics and the unanimity constraint. Provenance audit unverifiable in-sandbox; re-run host-side.

title: OECD says global minimum tax boosted revenue, not job losses
date_evidence:
By Thomson Reuters Jul 15, 2026 | 2:58 PM

PARIS, July 15 (Reuters) - Countries applying a global minimum tax on multinational companies saw corporate tax revenues rise
key_claim: Reuters reports the OECD's 2026 Economic Impact Assessment finding that the global minimum tax raised government revenue by 79 to 109 billion euro in its first year, equivalent to 2.4% to 3.4% of global corporate income tax receipts, below the pre-implementation projection of $155 billion to $192 billion a year, with limited evidence of effects on investment or employment.
frame_summary: This source argues that the global minimum tax is working as designed, raising revenue without measurable damage to investment or employment, and notes that the evidence predates the side-by-side arrangement exempting US-headquartered groups.
verbatim_quote: The Paris-based OECD estimated that the tax increased government revenue by €79 billion to €109 billion ($90 billion to $124 billion) in its first year, equivalent to 2.4% to 3.4% of global corporate income tax receipts.
verbatim_list: More ​than 60 countries and territories have implemented the ⁠rules, while many others ⁠are preparing to do so.

The revenue estimate ‌is below the OECD’s pre-implementation projection that the reform ⁠could eventually generate an additional $155 billion to $192 billion a ​year ‌in corporate tax revenue worldwide, reflecting that the study ​covers only ⁠the first year of implementation.
Applying to multinational ​groups with annual revenue above €750 million, the tax aims to ensure companies face ​an effective tax rate of at least 15% wherever they ‌operate.
notes: Reuters wire copy carried by WTVB; used as the accessible full-text record of the OECD 2026 Economic Impact Assessment released 15 July 2026, and as the sourced counter-argument. The captured quotes contain zero-width characters present in the live page. Provenance audit unverifiable in-sandbox; re-run host-side.
